They were with you in Travnik, and then you told them to go to the road that was 10 kilometres away to see whether the enemy was there, just carry out a check there. If ever the BH Army fires on you, you have to respond. So these are strict orders given by you. So they go to the road and, unfortunately, 10 kilometres from there they carry out abuse but you don't know about it, and when they return they say everything went fine, but it's not true what they told you. In such an eventuality, are you responsible for what happened or not? If we go by the rules, by the JNA, HVO rules, in your view would you be responsible for them or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Their commander is responsible, first and foremost, but I am co-responsible, because at the time they were in combat operations around the Travnik Brigade. As soon as I learn of a crime, whether he informed me or not, it is my responsibility to take steps in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So as soon as you hear of a crime being committed you have to take steps. And let us imagine that you hear nothing about them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If they leave the area of responsibility, my area of responsibility, I can't do anything. I can't undertake anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, but as part of your responsibility, don't you have the obligation once a military operation has been carried out to check whether your orders have been carried out properly or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, because throughout the time it is my duty to monitor the situation and to control the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. It's very clear. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And to conclude on this part, as I was saying a moment ago, if I could have the usher's assistance one more time, and I would like to have the three overheads, if you will, displays given IC numbers and have the witness please mark and date each of those, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can just sign what I've answered and what I've understood. Is it proper that I should sign the whole document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There seems to be a problem, because it is a document in English, Mr. Scott, and the witness does not speak English. You're asking him to sign a document that is not in his own language, so that's a problem, isn't it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Furthermore, furthermore, Mr. Scott, with maps we only accept that it be signed if the witness has done something to them. The witness hasn't done anything to these documents, so I think it's not proper that he sign it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If that's the Chamber's view, I understand that. My memory -- my memory would be somewhat different, and I would have thought that would have been the practice, but in the last four years -- or three and a half years we've marked all sorts of things, IC numbers, where the witness made no contribution whatsoever, so I was trying to get with the flow, if you will, and follow courtroom practice, but if that's the Chamber's view, I won't -- I will not persist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: No blame on you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: But you can ask an IC number.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I will. So I will give those -- extra copies to the usher, please, and just so we have it for the record. For the registrar's assistance, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the record, the three documents shall be given Exhibit IC01141, 01142, and 01143. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, I'm next going to direct your attention to the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And for the courtroom, I'm going to show -- and with reference to, for the record, Exhibit P11118, P11118. It is a video with an accompanying transcript. Because of time I'm only going to show or propose to only show the first couple of minutes of it because I think the overall video's approximately 20 minutes, and I don't want to take 20 minutes to play it, to be honest, but I'd like to show the first few minutes it and then go to a transcript to some specific -- one or two specific parts of the accompanying transcript, but perhaps the Chamber can get a flavour of it. So if we can play that. This is from the Kordic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, Mr. Filipovic, you may recall, because the same clip we showed to you in the Kordic case. It is a meeting, if you will, a public meeting on approximately the 16th of January, 1992, in connection with the declared independence of the State of Croatia in -- but the meeting taking place in Busovaca. Dario Kordic and others.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] To begin with, I will just say, I wish all of us the best with the Independent State of Croatia. "Long live Croatia."

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] French. French. I understand some French, but I'm getting French.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: We are getting B/C/S, so it's equality of arms.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't need the French, just to hear the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. Maybe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, I would -- I would suggest that we also hear the original, because we have subtitles. We don't need the translation, and it's nice to have the sound and atmosphere.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I was about to say the same thing with apologies to the translation booths. But I think we could just listen to it. We're only go to play the first couple of minutes anyway, unless the Chamber wants to see more. If we could just maybe play it again from the beginning, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can we stop there, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, then if you can turn in your binder to Exhibit -- by the same number, but you should find a transcript which is P11118. And I'm going to ask you, sir, if you can look for the -- about the fifth -- about the fifth intervention attributed to Dario Kordic if you will. You'll see at the very beginning Mr. Kordic speaks in the transcript, starts speaking, and again we see the audience reaction. If you continue on down several paragraphs, will you please find the portion that says: "Dario Kordic: When I said that the Croatian people waited for nine centuries ..." which is on the bottom of page 1 of the English transcript. Tell me, sir, when you've been able to find that.

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have it in my own language, but I did listen to what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It should be there. Well, then I'll read it to you and I'll have it translated. We'll see if -- I will read it, with my apologies. I will read it slowly, please, and ask for the booths to assist, please. "Dario Kordic: When I said that the Croatian people waited for nine centuries for this fulfilment, we must remember the tens of thousands of people who died and the dear lives, words inaudible, centuries for the Croatian state. Therefore, for all those who throughout centuries sacrificed their lives for their homeland and those couple of thousand Croats who lost their lives in this dirty war waged by the aggressor, the Greater Serbian Army against the Croatian nation, I would like us to observe a minute's silence for the sake of eternal peace for all those people, Croats who gave their lives for what we've experienced today. Dear lord may they rest in eternal peace," and then words apparently spoken by the audience inaudible. "Dario Kordic: Now that I have said some words about Busovaca to begin with, let me say that this Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, which includes Busovaca, also has the right to celebrate the big day of the realisation of the Croatian state. I would also like to say that today we are not becoming part of a Rump Yugoslavia in which there still remains four republics, that we here clearly and unambiguously say that the Croatian people will not be part of any other creation. This is Croatian soil and that is how it will be." The audience applauds. Sir, when that same clip was shown to you in the Kordic case, and you were questioned on this by Mr. Nice, you were asked whether you agreed and what your reaction to that speech would have been, and you testified in the Kordic case that you agreed and that had you been there you would have also applauded Mr. Kordic's speech; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the date was the 16th of January, 1992. Kordic was wearing civilian clothes. I do not see any flags or any problems there. I was in the JNA at the time, but this was after Vukovar. Unless I'm very much mistaken, this was a ceremony to mark the [as interpreted] recognition of the Croatian state by some 20 countries. Then as now, I have no objections to any of the words he uttered.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I react to the transcript, line 12. The witness said that this was a ceremony with respect to the international recognition of the Croatian state, and then I'd like to react to Mr. Scott's question on page 53 when he said that it was a ceremony of the proclamation of independence of the Republic of Croatia. It wasn't the proclamation of independence. It was just as the witness has said, the international recognition of the Republic of Croatia as a sovereign state.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I certainly accept that, Your Honour, and I certainly didn't mean to offend our Croatian friends or -- I'll accept that as a proper statement, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But, sir -- and so you agree that -- and as you testified in the Kordic case, and I'll just quote this particular part it again just so we're clear: "I would also have clapped my hands, applauded at this." And that's your position today as well; correct?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: As a professional soldier, sir, would you agree that an oath-taking ceremony, when a soldier joins and swears his oath of allegiance or what have you for the first time, that is an important part of a soldier's life?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Important for them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You also testified in the Kordic case under oath that you attended one or two HVO oath-taking ceremonies where Mr. Kordic was also present. Can you confirm that again today?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And on those occasions I take it that the soldiers -- the HVO soldiers who were taking the oath swore the statutory oath that is found in the Herceg-Bosna decree on armed forces which, for the record and which the Chamber has seen before, is Exhibit P00588. Let me read that to you, and can you -- perhaps you can confirm --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Actually, with the usher's assistance, I have one more piece of paper for the ELMO. Drop it down just a little bit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, this is the statutory oath that's found in Article 86 of the Herceg-Bosna decree on armed forces, which is the exhibit I referred to a moment ago, and I'll again -- once again I'll read it to you. Please listen to the translation, and I'll ask you a question or two. "I --"

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Just a moment, please. Your Honours, in the binder, the Prosecution binder, we do have this law. So I think it would be a good idea if the witness could read what it says for himself in Croatian, because it's easier when you read something for yourself rather than listen to something. So it's a document, P588, to be found in the middle of this binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I have no objection if that's -- the witness would be more comfortable with that on this occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness, if you can turn in your binder to P00588. It's a rather bulky document, and I was hopefully trying to save a few minutes of time, but we'll do it this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Perhaps the usher can assist. I'm sorry. P00588.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It's Article 86. Do you have it, sir?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I will nonetheless read it just for the record. You can follow along in Croatian. Decree on armed forces, Article 86: "I swear that I shall faithfully and honourably perform the duties required of me as a member of the Croatian Defence Council, and that I shall obey official commands and orders conscientiously and responsibly. I swear that I shall defend and protect my motherland of Herceg-Bosna, its sovereignty, territorial integrity, and all of its citizens even if my life is at stake." Now, sir is that -- on the occasions where you attended an HVO oath-taking, whether in the presence also of Mr. Kordic or on other occasions when you might have been at such an event without Mr. Kordic, is that the oath that was taken by the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that was the oath.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In your Kordic testimony, sir, you referred to Muslim soldiers, it appeared to be in a general way, not simply the 7th Muslim Brigade but in general as Mujahedin. And was that your view, sir, that all Muslim soldiers were Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, Mr. Scott is moving on to something else, but I would like to stay with this oath, because you said that you did take that oath, Article 86. I look at this article, and it seems that there is something missing here. Just -- a few words should have been added. There is no reference to the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Could you tell us why there is no mention of the following, it says: "I shall defend within the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina my motherland, my territory of Herceg-Bosna." Why is there no mention of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Do you have an explanation for this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Herceg-Bosnia is part of Bosnia-Herzegovina. There's no dilemma about that. On all documents it was written Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, then Herceg-Bosnia. Herceg-Bosnia specifically was a way to defend them -- for the Croats to defend themselves, to organise their life. Why there's no mention of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Well, in that Bosnia-Herzegovina we have the Republika Srpska. By that time we'd started fighting the army of Republika Srpska in Republika Srpska. For Bosnia-Herzegovina to exist one had to fight for it through Herceg-Bosna, therefore there is no dilemma for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Witness, what is your concept the term "sovereignty"? What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is state sovereignty. There are other sovereignties. But sovereignty is that in the territory or at home or anywhere else one can live freely, perform their duties. To live freely and to work freely. This is the concept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: So would you say that Alabama is a sovereign state?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Alabama?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is a state of the United States of America. It is sovereign within the US of A system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Here you find it necessary to specify within the United States. The oath does not specify within Bosnia and Herzegovina. That is what is -- is striking or remarkable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct. You were surprised in terms of Bosnia-Herzegovina sovereignty. For you the notion of Bosnia-Herzegovina is something which has its borders, which emerges, but for me Bosnia-Herzegovina is a framework for me to live in back in 1992 and today in 2009. Bosnia-Herzegovina is a sovereign state, but I, for instance, cannot enjoy anything in Republika Srpska. So Bosnia-Herzegovina is what it is. If it were -- is it ideal, can it be comparable to other states, that's another question altogether.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And would you today also say that Herceg-Bosna is a sovereign state?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It wasn't a state at the time either. It was Herceg-Bosna. It's a community of the Croatian people in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This was a means to survive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You're quite correct in correcting me. The word "state" does figure here, but would you say that today, I say carefully, Podrucje, the area of Herceg-Bosna is sovereign?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it's not. Today, for instance, we have the armed forces of the -- of Bosnia-Herzegovina. There's no ABiH, no HVO. There are the armed forces of the BiH. In 1992, Yugoslavia disintegrated and you had nothing, absolutely nothing. So how to organise, how to defend oneself. What to do. I wouldn't have minded for the text to read: "As a component of Bosnia-Herzegovina" or "for our Bosnia-Herzegovina," because it was. But Herceg-Bosnia was a way to self-organise, to survive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you're saying that it wouldn't have been a problem for you if there had been mention of Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Maybe the person who wrote the decree didn't see all these problems. I want to be fair with everyone. And please take a look at Article 106 of the same text. There is a reference made to the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina here. Can you confirm that there is mention of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, "... or other threats to Herceg-Bosnia, Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Republic of Croatia," et cetera. This is what I implied, and this is what is clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So under oath you are telling us that if the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina had been mentioned that wouldn't have bothered you? At least that's what I understood from what you said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we're discussing the soldiers' oath, it wouldn't have bothered me, but it didn't bother me in this way either because no reference was made to Montenegro but Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was implicitly known.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fair enough. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, you know, excuse me, sir, but it's all well and good for you to sit here today and say that in 2009, but when Mr. Kordic made his speech in 1992, the one that you said that if you had been there you would have applauded, he said nothing, he said absolutely nothing about this being part of Bosnia-Herzegovina. What he said was, in part, that: "We are here --" I'm referring to the part -- one of the parts I read to you a moment ago, "We here clearly and unambiguously say that the Croatian people will not be part of any other creation. This is Croatian soil and that is how it will be."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. No. [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think that there's no need for this. We will calm the situation down. Let's clarify very precisely what it's all about. This is January 1992, a time when Bosnia-Herzegovina is part of Yugoslavia or what was deemed Rump Yugoslavia after Slovenia and Croatia had left. We all know that one and a half months later, a referendum was established and that Bosnia-Herzegovina became an independent state only after that. What is Kordic is referring to is Yugoslavia. There is still no independent, sovereign, free Bosnia and Herzegovina as a state. Now, these are facts and this is an objection to your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm reading -- I'm reading the words off the page. I'm not interpreting or arguing a case. This is what Dario Kordic said. We can play the tape if they want to play the tape, but that's -- this is what it says and the rest is argument, and I understand, counsel can argue their case in the future if that's her interpretation but that's not the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, perhaps we should have assurance linguistically, because very often we have found that the terms -- that translation of terms is in dispute. I'm not saying that one side is right or the other. Mr. Kovacic, I think you wanted to refer to this; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I don't want to continue this argument, but if you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I don't want to continue this discussion, but it will help, just one word. It is a matter of what was said on video. Kordic said that appropriate moment this is about -- now I'm missing an English word. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I can help you. "This is Croatian soil. "

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, he said on English "Rump Yugoslavia." In Croatian, [Interpretation] "Rump Yugoslavia," [In English]; thus, he is clearly describing the situation exactly as Ms. Alaburic said. And I also want to join what Ms. Alaburic said. It is the fact. This is not argument. This is not discussion. We know the fact. We know and we have the evidence when the Bosnia-Herzegovina became independent state. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, I think we must give it to Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... it's an adjudicated fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And we must give it to Mr. Scott that at the end of the second paragraph of page 2 of this transcript we have here Kordic is reported as saying: "This is Croatian soil." So unless the Defence has good cause to say that it's the wrong translation, it is not correct to protest this. Please, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We will check in -- in the office -- we just got it. We were not able to -- to check the transcript. We will, of course, but I'm talking about what Kordic said on the tape. And when we were watching video, it was agreed that the witness also will be hearing original text, not the transcript. So it is in evidence. This is what it said. It might be requested from CLSS to do -- to do a proper transcript. It's not our duty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay. We must stop this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It is the duty of the party who submitted the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Scott go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The video is in evidence and -- my apologies, the video is in evidence, or at least it's being tendered - the entire video - and the Defence can play it as many times as they like. I'm happy -- I'm happy if there is a translation error, of course. The Prosecution does not want to put any evidence before the Chamber that there's a transcription -- a translation error, of course not, but we will deal with that. What I have in front of me - and what I've been assured is an accurate translation, there can be errors - is what it says in the part that we put to the witness, and there is nothing in that statement by Mr. Kordic that talks about being part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, nor is there anything in Article 86. And as I said now to go back to my question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It's all well and good, sir to, say sitting here in front of the Court in this particular circumstance in 2009 it wouldn't have bothered if some additional language had been added to the both but that's -- sorry, sir, we say the cow is out of the barn. In 1992 and 1993, this is the oath that was taken. This is the oath. You said so a while ago. You were at oath-takings and it was these were words, and it didn't say anything about being part of Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Taking an oath is a solemn occasion in any country of the world. So it was one in the case of the HVO then. There's no contention concerning Herceg-Bosnia in relation to Bosnia-Herzegovina, at least in my opinion. And the video footage of Mr. Kordic, from what I could judge on the basis of what I said, I could have applauded. I said that one -- ten years ago I would have said it the same. Croatian soil is Croatian soil, not Croatian state. It was my field, my road, my home. And in terms of notions that we hold, I see nothing contentious in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir if we go on then, in light of the -- in light of the things -- what's been said and the controversy that's been raised, let's go --

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm really sorry, but I think the transcript has to be corrected here. [Interpretation] On page 65, lines 13 and 14, the witness said in the sense this was an atmosphere that we lived in. We believe that notion that we hold is a mistranslation. He referred to the atmosphere in Bosnia and Herzegovina and the people's attitude towards the soil. I believe that the witness can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If it's a translation -- again if it's a transcription error, I certainly don't disagree.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, in light of what I was saying a moment ago and in light of things that have been said, let's continue on, then, in the transcript, and again I'll have to read it to you, and I apologise for there not being a Croatian version, but I will read to you a bit more. And now I'm turning to Mr. Kostroman, Mr. Kostroman being the second person who speaks, and I'm on page 3 in the English version middle of the page, Ignjac Kostroman, he starts by addressing the audience or the crowd after

utterances.speaker: MR. KORDIC IS FINISHED
utterances.text: "Dear citizens of the State of Croatia." In his -- the third paragraph below that: "Ignac Kostroman: We will build a state -- we shall build a state of citizens," et cetera. At the end of that intervention: "We are Croats and this is our Croatian state." Page 4 of the English version, middle of the page, Kostroman says: "I believe and maintain that we are an integral part of the State of Croatia." The audience applauds. Skip a line. "Ignac Kostroman: We will be an integral part of our dear State of Croatia by hook or by crook." Now, sir, would you also applaud those words?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way you interpreted them I would not. They were baseless. Kostroman can say whatever he wants and be responsible for his words. I don't want to comment, first of all, something I did not hear. I'm referring to what you say, how you interpret it, and I would not applaud to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's go back and let's -- let's go back to the question that I took you to some minutes ago now. In your Kordic testimony, sir, you referred at -- on some instances to Muslim soldiers as Mujahedin, and my question to you was: Was that a general term that you used for all Muslim soldiers, kind of like the Greens you said. Well, you didn't think Greens was really a derogatory term. And did you refer to all Muslim soldiers as Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I precisely knew who was Mujahedin. I felt the consequences of them being in that area, but far be it from me that I would call all Muslim soldiers Mujahedin. When we discuss the term the Greens, this was a brief way to describe the parties to the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And your testimony to the Chamber is that the only time you used the term "Mujahedin" was in reference to somebody that you considered to be a particular extremist or in a particular unit and that you did not use that term to describe Muslim generally. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I used the term "Mujahedin" for Mujahedin who were different from the others. It was clear who was Mujahedin and who was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, arising out of all this in the last few minutes and the Kordic speech, the Kostroman speech, the swear -- the oath that we talked about, you saw Mr. Kordic as a hero, didn't you, and you came to testify in his defence in The Hague because wanted to defend Mr. Kordic, defend him personally because you considered him a hero.

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, when I spoke yesterday of insinuations this is one of them. Kordic for me was never a hero. He was not a political leader that I would follow, come to speak of that. And my testimony is my individual attitude towards the Court to help the court take a very difficult decision in this and in other cases. I was an immediate witness, much more than others, and to put me into imagined groups or -- of individuals, this is -- I do not allow. I will answer any question, but this -- well, I understand this as condemnation. Why did you testify in Kordic? Why are you testifying in this case? I don't know how to take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you came and testified in Mr. Kordic's defence, claiming that he had no military power, no -- was not a military commander, had no military involvement in Central Bosnia. You came and you took that position under oath. You maintained that position when Mr. Nice showed you document after document demonstrating Mr. Kordic's military involvement, and you persisted in that, in your position, to defend Mr. Kordic, because you felt he was a hero; correct?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice called me a liar on several occasions in that case, but I ascribed that to the lack of proper procedures at this court. I repeat again: Kordic did not command in this operational zone of Central Bosnia, in the military district of Vitez. He could not have commanded it. I spoke so then, and I'm saying this now, and particularly I did not consider him to be a hero.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could I have the usher's assistance, please, to place another document on the ELMO. Drop down there, so we can see the top part, please. Maybe the whole -- maybe we can get the whole thing on there. Just about. Almost. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you testified to the positions that I've outlined briefly to you in the last few minutes. The Kordic Trial Chamber didn't find your evidence particularly persuasive. This is an excerpt -- these are excerpts from the actual judgement. It's an official record of this tribunal, and in paragraph 585 of the Trial Chamber's judgement the Kordic Chamber, the President in that case being Judge May, said: "On the other hand, the defence in answer to the Prosecution evidence about Mr. Kordic's role points to a number of milinfosums and other documents which refer to others as commander of the HVO in Busovaca in the relevant period, December 1992 to February 1993. The defence maintains that Kordic had no military power, did not and was not in a position to order military attacks. To this end, a great deal of evidence was called to show that Kordic played no military part in the conflict and simply wished to help his people: The defence relies on this evidence in respect of Kordic's alleged role in the Busovaca conflict." The Trial Chamber then in footnote 1069 listed the evidence that the Defence put forward to support that position. First among that evidence as you'll see here in footnote 1069, Major General Filip Filipovic. Now, let's contrast that Defence position in which you were cited in support of to the Trial Chamber's actual findings, paragraph 586. "The Trial Chamber finds that Dario Kordic was implicated in the attack on Busovaca as a leader exerting both political and military authority. The Trial Chamber draws this inference from the evidence of the audiotape, the documentary evidence, and the evidence of the accused's use of a headquarters and his control over the roads. The Trial Chamber is satisfied there is no truth in the evidence put forward by the Defence that the accused played no military part in the conflict and was simply helping his people." I put to you again, sir, and as demonstrated here by the Trial Chamber's assessment of your evidence, you came here to defend Mr. Kordic and gave evidence that was just totally contradicted by other evidence in the case, and you persisted in giving that evidence, taking your position even in the face of evidence that Mr. Nice put in front of you; correct?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, what was shown to me in that -- those proceedings, well, nothing which could indicate that I would have a separate opinion concerning a certain area. It cannot be that Kordic commanded in the military district of Vitez. He may have influence over certain commanders. He had some charisma and power in certain areas, but I can tell you this: He could not command in Travnik, in Vitez, in Novi Travnik. He could not issue in Zepce with Niko Lozancic, nothing in Kiseljak, in the area of Kiseljak. He could not command anybody. I don't know what the Trial Chamber found maybe on the basis of documents and testimonies, but what I can tell you is that Mr. Kordic did not command HVO units, and I will hold this opinion until I dead -- I die.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you considered, you personally considered the indictments against Mr. Kordic and Mr. Blaskic and others to be an act of political aggression, "political aggression [realtime transcript read in error "address"] by this Tribunal"; correct?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please tell me when I stated that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, perhaps you would like to turn to Exhibit P11131, P11131.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: In the meantime, the transcript is a bit watered down. It reads on line 20 of page 70, political address by this Tribunal. I think you spoke of aggression, not address. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Trechsel, it's aggression.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Aggression, a-g-g-r-e-s-s-i-o-n.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you have Exhibit P11131, sir, perhaps you'll recall an interview that you gave to the Croatian state news agency HINA in Zagreb, based in Zagreb, H-I-N-A, news agency Zagreb, as reported by the BBC news service, Novi Travnik, 18th of November: "The commander of the joint headquarters of the federal armed force of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Major General Filip Filipovic said yesterday that six leaders of Croat people in Central Bosnia, whom The Hague war Tribunal has indicted, were honest men. General Filipovic added that he believed that Croats in the Lasva Valley would resist as 'political aggression.'" Skipping down to the end of the article quoting you: "'To me this is the third aggression (following the Serbian and Muslim) against Croats in Central Bosnia. This one has been conducted by the international community,' General Filipovic said." That's your view. That was your view at the time. That was your view when you came to defend Mr. Kordic in his case, and that's your view today, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have an objection to that question, and I'd like to suggest that we define what indictments we're dealing with and who the six mean are accused before this Tribunal for a statement of this kind to be given, because otherwise joining up part of the story about Dario Kordic with this statement we could arrive in a situation where we don't know who we're talking about. Perhaps they were Croats who were accused but acquitted at this Tribunal. So which six leaders of the Croatian people give rise to this statement. THE PROSECUTOR: I'm most happy to assist. The six were Dario Kordic, Tihomir Blaskic, Mario Cerkez, Mr. Aleksovski, Pero Skopljak, and Ivan Santic. Mr. Kordic, Mr. Blaskic, Mr. Cerkez, and Mr. Aleksovski were all convicted following trial. Mr. Skopljak and Mr. Santic, the indictments were withdrawn by the Office of the Prosecutor and the case did not go forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Well, this is not quite correct information. The Prosecution said that those people were high-ranking HVO or HZ HB functionaries in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is not correct. Five of them are definitively only related to very limited area of Central Bosnia. Better to say one of municipality in Central Bosnia and that is Vitez. Mr. Kordic only is perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Only.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: -- a little bit on the higher level, but not other five. And beside, many others were indicted in the same or very similar indictment. Some of them acquitted even -- even before the trial starts and some during the trial. This is not, of course, mentioned. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And to what end? That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It shows that it is very different. Sometimes you got the case and sometimes not. So it doesn't look like it was black and white. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Kovacic, but that's -- to the extent you're casting aspersions on the Office of the Prosecutor on this Tribunal, that's just not correct. It was a quite entirely ethical and entirely responsible; in fact, not political aggression at all. The fact that the Office of the Prosecutor had the good ethical and honest sense to withdraw certain indictments as not sufficiently supported was not a political decision, it was a legal one, and the reality is that Mr. Kordic was convicted. He was the most important -- this man, in fact, testified in the Kordic case that he was the most important politician in Central Bosnia. He was no small fish. Mr. Blaskic the head of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, one of the four most senior officers below the Main Staff and all of the HVO, no small fish, and he was convicted. There were four of them convicted and two of the indictments with withdrawn, and I'm happy to say that. I feel no doubt or question about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't expect such a rude respond. Let's take Blaskic as an example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry, I think -- I think this -- this is rather distracted and taking the attention away from what is at issue. I think Mr. Scott has first put this interview to the witness and now asks him whether he has the same attitude today, and I think that's a proper question and whether the -- how high ranking the others were, this is really not relevant. It doesn't help, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I entirely agree with exactly what you said, but then he should ask on that way, but the Prosecutor is trying to create artificially and without base atmosphere in which the witness has no other choice but to say, well, yes, sir. I mean, this is -- this is kind of pressure to the witness. And by the way --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: -- factual representations by the Prosecutor should be guarded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... Mr. Kovacic --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... for example, the last thing that he said for Blaskic, Blaskic is on the end sentenced and tried for -- well -- allow me licensa poetica. For a traffic offence in comparison what he was indicted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So he was not [overlapping speakers] a big fish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, I quite agree that the witness is put under pressure. I absolutely agree with you. I share this observation. But, Mr. Kovacic, this is the essence of cross-examination. It is a very unpleasant exercise whether exercised by Defence or by the public prosecutor. Unfortunately, this is the system that is applied here. So I think we should allow Mr. Scott to go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: -- this pressure on cross should have a very, very sensitive border. We cannot be too aggressive. On the end, we depends on the witnesses. I wonder who we will get in the future. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, here in these trial proceedings we're not having again Blaskic or Kordic at the accused stand. We're not retrying them here. Just one technical point submitted by the Prosecutor regarding you. It was the part, the military part that Mr. Kordic possibly played. You said no, Kordic was a political man and had no military role. That is what you say. And I was listening to you, but always thinking, because I don't hide anything. I'm absolutely 100 per cent transparent for everybody, for the Prosecution, for the witness or the Defence. It's absolute transparency on my part. So I take the Prosecution case. The Prosecutor says that Kordic had a military role. So I translate -- I'm trying to put him in the chain of command. As I understood it, we have Mr. Blaskic, and you told us that in the four operative zones you were in the Vitez Operative Zone. So I'm wondering whether -- assuming that Kordic has a military role where he would be in this chain of command. Where could he be placed in theory? Would he be at your level or close to -- next to Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, let me clarify. In the context of Kordic and my testimony here in the Kordic trial, I was -- it was said that I had said -- or that's how I understood it, that I had used this political aggression or whatever, and then a newspaper article is pulled out from 1995 and presented to me, and as I heard presented here, it said -- well, what I want to say is that the conduct towards me is improper. If that is proper procedure at this Tribunal, then fine. I've become accustomed to living under pressure, but it is improper on the part of the professional sitting here in the courtroom. That's my opinion. You can't conduct a trial in that fashion. You can't speak about Kordic, exhibits, my testimony during the Kordic trial, and then use the term "political aggression" taken from a newspaper article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I asked you a question. It was a technical question that does not call for any comments. So I have the Prosecution case which I compared to your position. The Prosecutor insists on saying that Kordic had a military role. So that's the Prosecutor's case. And you say I don't agree with it. So I'm trying to really sort of see what is truth in all this. I try to understand everybody's position and I'm asking you this: If Kordic had any military role, where would he be positioned in the chain of command, at your level or next to Mr. Blaskic. This is what I'm trying to understand, you see.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: General Filipovic, I also would like to say the following: As a matter of fact, I do not want to be, of course, kind of a teacher for you and also I would like to be very transparent, but I would like to tell you that now here you are not here to tell us and to tell the Prosecution what kind of questions you would like to answer, but as my fellow Judge, Judge Trechsel, a few minutes ago explained to you, you are to be here, as a matter of fact, to answer the questions according to your best knowledge and -- and in a fashion which, of course, quite -- should be quite -- to have equilibrium. You may say that do you not know about it. You may say that you do not understand the question. You may say that you do not agree with it, but you -- your opinion, this or that, but anyway, you have to answer the questions. It is the rule of the game, and I hope you will understand it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So please answer my question. Otherwise, we're getting lost.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've said many times Kordic did not command. He's not in the chain of command, and you can't put him anywhere in the chain of command, absolutely nowhere. I think that's a concrete answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So he was nowhere. I hail from a country that is mainly characterised by logics, and so I'm thinking aloud here in front of you. Mr. Blaskic was tried. Mr. Kordic was tried too. You are a mere witness never you -- were you indicted or convicted for anything. But let us take Mr. Blaskic and Mr. Kordic. You, at any rate, you would be in the chain of command but only under them, because you cannot be put between Kordic and Blaskic otherwise you would have been tried too. Is that wrong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was the number two man in the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia below Blaskic. That's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're telling us that in Blaskic's operative zone you were number two, so there cannot be anybody between you and Blaskic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, there couldn't have been anybody between me and Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. You see, I'm trying to understand from what a logical point of view. I'm trying to understand why Blaskic and Kordic were indicted in a case whilst the number two was not, because you were the number two. At least that's what you say. Unless we think that Mr. Kordic was number two and you were number three. But you say no, no, no, you were number two. I don't know whether this shed any light on your case, Mr. Scott. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I know that when we come to cross-examination, as Judge Trechsel said, it is legitimate to exert pressure on the witness; however, I think that regardless of the fact that there is pressure it must be fair pressure. Now, if we are putting to the witness an alleged statement of his given to some interview to some journalist, we have to establish first of all what this was and say that was your position then, now, and what will it be in future? We heard it earlier on in the Kordic trial. So this is something that was carried by the BBC, taken from the Croatian news agency HINA. Now, HINA could have taken the article from any journalist, perhaps from Bosnia-Herzegovina. So I think it would be fair to ask the witness whether he remembers giving this interview in the first place and whether he remembers saying that. And then, once we hear the answer, the Prosecutor can go ahead and ask him if that is his position, and then the Defence counsel can prepare themselves to re-examine, so we need to know who the author of this article is and who it is who claims that Mr. Filipovic said what said -- made this statement in this article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think we have a witness before us who is controlled, intelligent, courageous, and I have the confidence that he would have said immediately, "I never said that," but he did not. So I think, Mr. Scott -- Mr. Scott, I think you should continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You should sit over there and see what kind of pressure is upon you. I do have some rights here, Your Honour. First of all, the Prosecutor conveyed this completely erroneously. The Prosecutor first of all put Kordic's statement where he said we're not going to stay in a Rump Yugoslavia at the time when Bosnia-Herzegovina was in Yugoslavia and Izetbegovic made the agreement, and it is up to this Tribunal to establish the truth. There are so many lies stated here and so much pressure is exerted that it's a catastrophe, and that's what it is, Judge Trechsel. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, whenever sensitive issues are addressed by the Prosecution, you react to them. You've just said that the Prosecutor misstated, mischaracterised Kordic's words. It may be right, it may be wrong, but there's one thing you should not forget. This witness is a witness for the Petkovic Defence. The Petkovic Defence called this witness to testify. Next week they will have time for redirect. Obviously, if the Petkovic Defence is of the view that the Prosecutor mischaracterised those words, it will say so automatically. So please let the lawyers do their jobs, because this witness is not your witness. He is a witness for General Petkovic. So let the lawyers do their work. If Ms. Alaburic feels that there's been mischaracterisation, she will say so, and there will always be time to change and correct things. I don't know. We saw some video footage. We saw people applauding, shouting Croatia, Croatia. I've seen a lady in tears. Obviously, it was a very important moment. I've heard the Defence say that this video footage had to be put back in the then context, which was a context of the independence of the Republic of Croatia. I also have seen that Mr. Kordic spoke about Germany, thanked Germany. We all know that Germany was one of the very first countries to recognise the independent country of the Republic of Croatia. I've also seen that Mr. Kordic spoke about the Pope and thanked the Pope as well. So this is what I have read in the statement. The Prosecutor has his own view, his own take on things. That's his job and that's what he's doing as part of the cross-examination, and the witness can say no, I don't agree with you Prosecutor. That's what the witness has not stopped saying. So why do you have to speak on top of that? The Judges are here. They listen. They can read. I don't think we're dumb. Well, I hope and I claim I'm not dumb. I may be wrong, but, please, let us work in peace. You see, I put questions before in order to see where Kordic could be positioned, because the Prosecutor said that he was a military man, and if he is, he should be in a chain of command. And the witness said, "Well, there was number one Blaskic, and then number two it was me." So please stay calm, because you really jump out of your box, and I think you're going to have a heart attack. You frighten me. Please calm down and let the lawyers do their work. You've got excellent lawyers. Everybody's excellent, so let them do their work. And sometimes we ask you to take the floor. You're allowed to ask questions of witnesses. Well, maybe not for this one because you've done it already, but next time you could revisit the issue and say, "Well, yes, this was said," so you can tackle the topic again. This is what I wanted to tell you, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I do hope that I will have a heart attack. I sincerely hope so, whether you believe me or not, precisely because -- well, you say untruths. I'm saying lies, and I want that to be crystal clear. Lies were stated there. The Defence counsel didn't hear properly what Kordic said. I'm sitting far away from the counsel. Erroneous facts cannot be presented at this Tribunal whether it be done by the Prosecution or whoever, and if somebody has portrayed something erroneously, then he must be cautioned and told.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I believe that we need for the situation to cool down. We should all stay collected, prepare for the rest of the questions. I believe Ms. Alaburic also must also prepare for her redirect. Our witness probably needs to have a rest. He's been in the witness seat for three days now, and it's very tiring to answer questions all the time. I believe that next week will be -- we'll finish this witness, and then -- well, I believe Mr. Scott has about an hour left for his cross-examination. I can tell you exactly how much time he has left. So far you have used two hours and 31 minutes, so you have one hour and 30 minutes left. We're sitting for four hours tomorrow. I believe that between the cross-examination and the redirect we should be finished with this witness, and then we'll have the other witness for Tuesday and Wednesday. That's just to give you an idea for the schedule for next week. Ms. Alaburic, do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know whether there was a mistake, but we do not have any information whereby we would be working tomorrow. Tomorrow is Friday. We're not working tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: It was Monday, not tomorrow. Interpreter's correction: Monday, not tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we'll continue on Monday. Monday Mr. Scott will have one hour and 30 minutes left. Then we'll have the redirect. So, Witness, your testimony will be over on Monday, and then we'll have another witness for Tuesday and Wednesday. Witness, remember my advice -- my instructions, actually. You're not supposed to contact anyone. And I wish everyone a pleasant evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 7th day of December, 2009, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 5.55 p.m.,
